title: South Africa’s fuel outlook and Vopak’s investment case
columns:
Demand remains substantial: 21.94bn litres of petrol and diesel sold in 2023. Petrol declined over 2013–2023 while diesel grew slowly.

Refinery closures increased import dependence. In 2025, gross imports reached 16.70bn litres; Durban customs accounted for 13.16bn litres.

Durban–NMPP–Lesedi connects imports to inland customers. Gauteng’s 6.81bn-litre demand provides context (2022); delivered cost and access define Vopak’s reachable market.

Demand drivers can reverse. Eskom’s own OCGT fuel use fell 40% in FY2025. Rail recovery, EVs/HEVs and efficiency affect fuel demand; GDP and fuel prices affect activity and travel.

Domestic supply can change. SAPREF, Secunda’s gas/MRG choices and Natref require dated output scenarios; refinery capacity alone cannot determine imports.

Vopak’s route must compete with road/rail from Durban and supply via Matola or Walvis Bay on delivered cost, access and reliability.

Establish Vopak’s current share and additional capture by product, customer and destination. Reconcile shared Durban–Lesedi transfers to count unique demand once.

The new illustrative base gives Durban 2.63bn litres, including 1.32bn through Lesedi. It assumes 20% import capture and 50% onward routing; actual share remains open.

Test working tanks, turns and dispatch first. New investment depends on secured incremental flows, a capacity shortfall and returns that withstand downside cases.
